Plaintiff, appearing pro se, alleges:

## I. Nature of the Action

1. Defendant is a Member of Congress. She maintains an account on X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, at [[ACCOUNT URL]] (the "Account"), and uses it to conduct official business, including announcing votes, describing committee action, publicizing district events, and communicating with constituents.

2. The Account is open to the public. Any X user may read its posts, reply to them, repost them, and quote them. Defendant has not limited who may reply.

3. Plaintiff is a constituent. On [[DATE OF PLAINTIFF'S POST]], Plaintiff replied to a post on the Account, writing: "[[TEXT OF PLAINTIFF'S POST]]."

4. On [[DATE OF BLOCK]], Defendant blocked Plaintiff from the Account. Blocking is not a rule applied to a comment; it is a status imposed on a person. While signed in, Plaintiff can no longer view the Account's posts, reply to them, repost them, or participate in the comment threads beneath them.

5. Defendant blocked Plaintiff because of the viewpoint Plaintiff expressed. Other users who replied to the same posts, including users whose criticism was sharper than Plaintiff's, remain unblocked.

6. The exclusion violates the First Amendment. Plaintiff seeks a declaration that the block is unconstitutional and an injunction requiring Defendant to restore Plaintiff's access and to refrain from viewpoint-based blocking of Plaintiff.

7. Plaintiff seeks no money damages. The relief sought is declaratory and injunctive only.

## II. Parties

8. Plaintiff [[PLAINTIFF FULL NAME]] is a citizen of the United States residing at [[STREET ADDRESS]], [[CITY]], [[STATE]] [[ZIP]]. Plaintiff appears pro se. Plaintiff's electronic-mail address is [[EMAIL]] and telephone number is [[TELEPHONE]].

9. Plaintiff is a constituent of Defendant and, at all relevant times, held the X account @[[PLAINTIFF HANDLE]].

10. Defendant [[MEMBER FULL NAME]] is the [[MEMBER TITLE]] for [[DISTRICT DESCRIPTION]]. She is sued in her official capacity only and may be served at [[MEMBER OFFICE ADDRESS]].

## III. Jurisdiction and Venue

11. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, because this action arises under the Constitution of the United States.

12. Venue is proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2), because a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim — Plaintiff's speech, the block, and the resulting deprivation of access — occurred in this district, where Plaintiff resides and reads the Account.

13. Venue is also proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(e)(1), which permits an action against an officer of the United States acting in an official capacity to be brought in the district where the plaintiff resides, if no real property is involved.

14. The Court may grant declaratory relief under 28 U.S.C. § 2201 and further necessary relief under 28 U.S.C. § 2202.

15. This action does not ask the Court to question anything Defendant said or did in the exercise of legislative functions. It challenges the administration of a public comment channel, which is not a legislative act. *See United States v. Brewster*, 408 U.S. 501, 515–16 (1972); *Hutchinson v. Proxmire*, 443 U.S. 111, 130 (1979).

## IV. Facts

### A. The Account Is an Official Account

16. The Account's display name is "[[DISPLAY NAME]]" and its handle is @[[ACCOUNT HANDLE]]. Its biography states: "[[BIOGRAPHY TEXT]]."

17. The Account is linked from Defendant's official congressional website, [[OFFICIAL WEBSITE URL]], under the heading "[[LINK TEXT]]."

18. The Account announces official business. On [[DATE]], for example, it announced [[DESCRIBE OFFICIAL ANNOUNCEMENT]]. A true copy is attached as Exhibit [[A]].

19. The Account is operated by Defendant's official staff. [[DESCRIBE: posts are written by staff; the account responds to casework inquiries; the account's content tracks the office's press releases.]]

20. The Account is not a campaign account. It bears no "Paid for by" disclaimer and solicits no contributions.

### B. Plaintiff Spoke on a Matter of Public Concern

21. On [[DATE OF DEFENDANT'S POST]], Defendant posted [[DESCRIBE THE POST]].

22. Plaintiff replied: "[[TEXT OF PLAINTIFF'S POST]]." A true copy is attached as Exhibit [[B]].

23. Plaintiff's reply addressed Defendant's conduct of her office. It contained no threat, no disclosure of personal information, no obscenity, and no solicitation.

### C. Defendant Blocked Plaintiff

24. On [[DATE OF BLOCK]], Plaintiff attempted to open the Account and was shown the message "[[BLOCK MESSAGE]]." A true copy is attached as Exhibit [[C]].

25. Since that date, while signed in as @[[PLAINTIFF HANDLE]], Plaintiff cannot view the Account's posts, reply to them, repost them, or read the comment threads beneath them.

26. Plaintiff has not been unblocked.

### D. The Block Was Based on Viewpoint

27. Other users replied to the same post with criticism of Defendant. Those replies remain visible and those users remain unblocked.

28. On information and belief, the user @[[OTHER USER HANDLE]] wrote "[[COMPARABLE OR HARSHER COMMENT]]," and remains able to reply to the Account. A true copy is attached as Exhibit [[D]].

29. Defendant has published no rule governing who may comment on the Account.

### E. Injury

30. Plaintiff can no longer read the Account's announcements of votes, committee action, and district events — information Defendant distributes there, and in some instances distributes nowhere else in a timely manner.

31. Plaintiff can no longer address the audience that gathers beneath the Account's posts, which includes other constituents, reporters, and Defendant's staff.

32. Plaintiff can no longer petition Defendant in the channel Defendant created for public response to her official business.

## V. Count One — Viewpoint Discrimination in Violation of the First Amendment

33. Plaintiff realleges paragraphs 1 through 32.

34. Defendant acted under color of federal authority. She possessed actual authority to speak on behalf of her office, and she exercised that authority on the Account. *See Lindke v. Freed*, 601 U.S. 187, 198 (2024).

35. The comment space beneath the Account's posts is a public forum. Defendant intentionally opened it for public discussion by using the Account as an official vehicle for governance and by making its interactive features available to the public without limitation. *See Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump*, 928 F.3d 226, 236 (2d Cir. 2019).

36. Defendant excluded Plaintiff from that forum because of the viewpoint Plaintiff expressed.

37. Viewpoint discrimination is barred in every forum. *Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc.*, 473 U.S. 788, 806 (1985); *Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of the University of Virginia*, 515 U.S. 819, 829 (1995).

38. Defendant has no compelling interest that justifies the exclusion, and no content-neutral rule that explains it. Avoiding criticism is not a governmental interest the First Amendment recognizes.

39. The availability of workarounds does not cure the violation. A blocked user's ability to log out, search, or post elsewhere does not restore access to the forum from which she was excluded. *See Knight*, 928 F.3d at 234.

## VI. Count Two — Denial of the Right to Petition

40. Plaintiff realleges paragraphs 1 through 39.

41. The First Amendment secures the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances," and that right "extends to all departments of the Government." *California Motor Transport Co. v. Trucking Unlimited*, 404 U.S. 508, 510 (1972).

42. By opening the Account's comment space and using it to discuss official business, Defendant invited petitions from constituents. Plaintiff's reply was such a petition.

43. Blocking Plaintiff from that channel denies the petition.

## VII. Count Three — Conduct Beyond Statutory Authority

44. Plaintiff realleges paragraphs 1 through 43.

45. No statute, rule of the House or Senate, or regulation authorizes a Member of Congress to exclude a constituent from an official communications channel because of the constituent's viewpoint.

46. An officer who acts beyond the authority conferred on her acts individually and may be enjoined. *See Larson v. Domestic & Foreign Commerce Corp.*, 337 U.S. 682, 689 (1949).

47. The exclusion is therefore both unconstitutional and ultra vires.

## VIII. Prayer for Relief

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court:

A. Declare that Defendant's block of Plaintiff from the Account violates the First Amendment;

B. Enjoin Defendant, her officers, agents, employees, and successors in office from blocking Plaintiff from the Account, and from enforcing against Plaintiff any policy or practice of blocking users because of the viewpoints they express;

C. Order Defendant to restore Plaintiff's access to the Account within seven days of the Court's order;

D. Retain jurisdiction to enforce the order; and

E. Grant such other relief as justice requires.

Plaintiff does not request money damages.
